entry.title: Would you want to know if Ghostface is at your door?

media:group.media:title: Would you want to know if Ghostface is at your door?
media:group.media:description:
Would you want to know if Ghostface is at your door? New AI-powered text descriptions on Ring, Nest, and Apple Home-compatible video doorbells claim to tell you exactly what's happening on your porch without making you wait for a video clip to buffer. I put them to the test to see how smart they are, and if any of them could catch Ghostface. Read my full review at theverge.com.

entry.title: Meta’s Muse actually does the thing | The Vergecast

media:group.media:title: Meta’s Muse actually does the thing | The Vergecast
media:group.media:description:
Meta's Muse AI agent is cute (sometimes caked-up) and it performs well as a productivity tool. And, if you give it access to your social media and e-mail, it can know basically everything about you. This week on The Vergecast, Nilay Patel, Jake Kastrenakes and David Imel give their reactions to Mark Zuckerberg's demos at Wednesday's Meta Connect keynote. They also talk about the new glasses hardware, including the new VR glasses and audio-only, camera-free Ray-Bans.
Then, we take a look at the newly-announced, chimeric Chrome/Android hybrid Googlebooks, find out why Brendan Carr is a dummy this week, analyze the Paramount merger, discuss what YouTube's A/B video testing means for the increasingly tenuous concept of a shared reality, and end on a surprisingly heartwarming story about RODECaster 4K support.

media:group.media:title: Meta Connect Impressions
media:group.media:description:
Senior reporters Victoria Song and Jay Peters give a recap of their experience at Meta Connect, from Meta's Muse AI charm to Meta’s new line of glasses: new audio-only Ray-Bans, Ray-Ban Gen 3, and Meta Glasses.
Meta does have a couple of minor privacy updates — the first is bringing the same “private processing” pipeline used on WhatsApp to wearables. It’s a server-based system in which a user’s data is inaccessible to Meta or any other third parties when end-to-end encryption isn’t possible or on-device processing isn’t powerful enough. The other is the ability for users to opt out of their visual data being used for AI training. (Audio-only queries are still used for training.)
